title: Real-Time PCR Quantification: Ct, Efficiency, ΔΔCt and Digital PCR
summary: Read Ct values (lower Ct = more template), calculate efficiency from a standard-curve slope and fold-change from ΔCt, apply 2^−ΔΔCt, explain why SYBR Green needs a melt curve, and know why digital PCR needs no standard curve.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 69 Hits 1, 2, 3, 9 and 12 and Traps 1, 3 and 5. Checked against Kralik 2017, Cikos 2007, Kockerols 2020, Mirabile 2024 and Tajadini 2014. The reviewer’s “E = 10^(−1/slope), perfect at 2.0” is the amplification-factor convention; Kralik reports efficiency as 10^(−1/slope) − 1 (1 = 100%). Both are taught. The exact Poisson formula is not taught (not in the sources read).

objectives: Interpret Ct values and the standard curve (lower Ct = more template).
Calculate amplification factor/efficiency from a slope and fold-change from ΔCt or ΔΔCt.
Explain SYBR Green non-specificity and the principle of digital PCR.

scenes.title: Ct 22 or Ct 31: which has more virus?
scenes.altText: Two real-time PCR wells (schematic amplification curves): Sample A crosses the threshold at cycle 22, Sample B at cycle 31. A third well glows with SYBR Green but has no template. Question token: “Which sample has more target — and why does the no-template well glow?”

cues.text: Two patient samples run in real-time PCR. Sample A crosses the threshold at cycle 22; sample B at cycle 31.
A no-template control with SYBR Green dye also glows late in the run.
Which sample started with more target, how much more, and why does a well with no template glow?

props.label: More target? How much? Why the glow?

scenes.title: Each cycle multiplies the target
scenes.altText: An equation card: Nn = N0 × (1 + E)^n (Kralik 2017), where E = 1 (100%) means doubling each cycle. Definition card: Ct (Cq) is the cycle at which fluorescence first rises above the threshold. A schematic standard curve: Ct plotted against log10 of starting copies from 10-fold dilutions is a straight line sloping downward; at 100% efficiency each 10-fold step shifts Ct by 3.32 cycles (slope −3.32). Token: more starting template → lower Ct.

cues.text: PCR is exponential. After n cycles, the copy number is the starting number times one plus the efficiency, raised to the power n. At 100 percent efficiency, the target doubles every cycle.
The threshold cycle, Ct, also called Cq, is the cycle at which fluorescence first rises above the threshold.
Run 10-fold dilutions of a standard and plot Ct against the log of the starting amount: the line slopes downward. At 100 percent efficiency, each 10-fold step moves the Ct by 3.32 cycles.
So the relationship is inverted: more starting template crosses the threshold earlier and gives a lower Ct. Ct is inversely related to the log of the starting amount.

props.title: Standard curve (schematic)
lines: Ct vs log10 copies: slopes down

scenes.title: Efficiency and fold-change
scenes.altText: Efficiency card: from the standard-curve slope, amplification factor = 10^(−1/slope) (2.0 = perfect doubling); efficiency % = (10^(−1/slope) − 1) × 100. Worked values: slope −3.32 → factor 2.00, 100%; slope −3.6 → 1.90, ~90%; slope −3.1 → 2.10, ~110%. Fold-change card: a sample crossing 3 cycles earlier has factor³ more template — 2³ = 8× at perfect efficiency, 1.96³ ≈ 7.5×. ΔΔCt card (2^−ΔΔCt, Livak; assumes 100% efficiency): ΔCt = Ct target − Ct reference gene; ΔΔCt = ΔCt sample − ΔCt calibrator. Example: sample 24 − 18 = 6; calibrator 27 − 18 = 9; ΔΔCt = −3; 2^3 = 8-fold higher. Pfaffl’s model corrects for efficiency ≠ 100%.

cues.text: The standard-curve slope gives the efficiency. The amplification factor is 10 to the power of minus one over the slope; 2.0 means perfect doubling. Subtract 1 and multiply by 100 for percent efficiency.
A slope of minus 3.32 gives 100 percent. Minus 3.6 gives about 90 percent; minus 3.1 gives about 110 percent.
A sample crossing 3 cycles earlier has the amplification factor cubed times more template: 8 times at perfect doubling, about 7.5 times at a factor of 1.96.

For relative expression, the 2 to the minus delta-delta Ct method first subtracts a reference gene’s Ct from the target’s, then subtracts the calibrator’s delta Ct. Here, 6 minus 9 is minus 3, so the sample has 2 cubed, 8 times more.
That method assumes 100 percent efficiency. Pfaffl’s model corrects for efficiencies that differ from the ideal.

scenes.title: Dyes, melt curves and digital PCR
scenes.altText: SYBR Green card: binds the minor groove of any double-stranded DNA and fluoresces about 1,000-fold more when bound; primer-dimers and non-specific products also glow, appearing as extra peaks on the dissociation (melt) curve. Probe card: hydrolysis (TaqMan) probes add sequence specificity. Digital PCR card: the sample is split into thousands of partitions (e.g., ~20,000 droplets), each amplified to an endpoint and scored positive or negative; a Poisson correction accounts for partitions holding more than one copy; no calibrated standard curve is needed → absolute quantification, less sensitive to efficiency differences. Back to the hook: A (Ct 22) has more target: 9 cycles earlier ≈ 2⁹ = 512× at 100% efficiency; the no-template glow is most likely primer-dimer seen by SYBR Green.

cues.text: SYBR Green binds any double-stranded DNA and fluoresces about a thousand times more when bound. That includes primer-dimers and non-specific products.
A melt curve exposes them as extra peaks. Hydrolysis probes such as TaqMan add sequence specificity instead.
Digital PCR splits the sample into thousands of partitions, amplifies each to the end, and scores each positive or negative. A Poisson correction allows for partitions holding more than one copy.
Because it counts, digital PCR needs no calibrated standard curve: it gives absolute quantification and is less affected by efficiency differences.

Back to the hook: sample A crossed 9 cycles earlier, about 2 to the ninth, 512 times more target at perfect efficiency. The late glow in the no-template well is most likely primer-dimer seen by SYBR Green; a melt curve would confirm it.

props.label: A: 9 cycles earlier ≈ 512× · NTC glow: likely primer-dimer

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Ct 35 means more template than Ct 30” (✓ higher Ct = less template); “SYBR Green is sequence-specific” (✓ binds any dsDNA; use a melt curve or a probe); “Digital PCR needs a standard curve” (✓ partition, count, Poisson-correct: absolute quantification).

cues.text: Trap one: a Ct of 35 means more template than 30. No: a higher Ct means less starting template; it took longer to cross the threshold.
Trap two: SYBR Green is sequence-specific. No: it binds any double-stranded DNA; specificity comes from the primers, checked by a melt curve, or from a probe.
Trap three: digital PCR needs a standard curve. No: it partitions, counts positives and applies a Poisson correction for absolute quantification.

props.title: ✗ “SYBR Green is sequence-specific.”
lines: ✓ Any dsDNA → melt curve or probe

scenes.title: Early bird has the most worms
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The early bird has the most worms”: the sample that crosses the threshold earliest (lowest Ct) started with the most target; every 3.3 cycles ≈ 10-fold. Tokens: Low Ct = lots · 3.3 cycles = 10× · 1 cycle = 2×. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the early bird has the most worms. The sample crossing the threshold earliest, with the lowest Ct, started with the most target. About 3.3 cycles is a 10-fold difference; one cycle is 2-fold.
Where it breaks: those numbers assume 100 percent efficiency; inhibitors delay the Ct without less target; and Ct values are not comparable between different assays or instruments.

props.text: Early bird = most worms (lowest Ct = most target)

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Lower Ct = more template · slope −3.32 = 100% · factor = 10^(−1/slope) · ΔCt 3 → factor³”, “2^−ΔΔCt normalizes to a reference gene and calibrator · SYBR binds any dsDNA → melt curve · digital PCR: no standard curve”.

cues.text: Lower Ct means more starting template, the standard-curve slope gives efficiency, SYBR Green needs a melt curve, and digital PCR counts partitions without a standard curve.

props.label: Lower Ct = more template · slope −3.32 = 100% · 3 cycles = factor³
2^−ΔΔCt: reference gene + calibrator · SYBR → melt curve · dPCR: no curve

explanation.what: Plain language: real-time PCR watches the product build up each cycle; the earlier the signal crosses a threshold, the more target the sample started with. Scientific terms: threshold cycle (Ct/Cq), amplification efficiency, standard curve, 2^−ΔΔCt (comparative Ct), reference gene, calibrator, SYBR Green, melt (dissociation) curve, hydrolysis probe, digital PCR, Poisson correction.
explanation.why: PCR is exponential (Nn = N0 × (1 + E)^n), so a sample with more starting copies reaches the detection threshold in fewer cycles. Efficiency determines how much each cycle multiplies the product. Intercalating dyes report any dsDNA, so non-specific products also generate signal. Digital PCR counts positive partitions rather than reading a curve.
explanation.measure: Standard curve of Ct vs log10 amount from 10-fold dilutions: slope −3.32 = 100% efficiency (factor 2.0); factor = 10^(−1/slope), efficiency = factor − 1. A sample 3 cycles earlier has factor³ more template (8× at 2.0; 7.53× at 1.96). 2^−ΔΔCt: ΔCt = Ct target − Ct reference; ΔΔCt = ΔCt sample − ΔCt calibrator; assumes 100% efficiency (Pfaffl corrects). Digital PCR: thousands of partitions, positive/negative, Poisson correction, no calibrated standard curve.
explanation.differs: Real-time PCR quantifies against a standard curve or relative to a reference gene; digital PCR gives absolute counts without a curve. SYBR Green (any dsDNA; needs a melt curve) vs hydrolysis probes (sequence-specific).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which Ct means more template, efficiency from slope, fold-change for a ΔCt, a ΔΔCt calculation, why SYBR Green needs a melt curve, and digital PCR without a standard curve.

questions.stem: In the same real-time PCR assay, sample X has a Ct of 25 and sample Y a Ct of 28. Assuming 100% efficiency, how do their starting amounts compare?

options.text: X has about 8 times more target than Y
options.rationale: Correct. X crossed 3 cycles earlier; at doubling per cycle that is 2³ = 8-fold more.

options.text: Y has about 8 times more target than X
options.rationale: Incorrect. A higher Ct means less starting template.

options.text: X has 3 times more target than Y
options.rationale: Incorrect. The difference is exponential (2³), not linear.

options.text: X has about 1,000 times more target

questions.stem: A standard curve of Ct versus log10 copies has a slope of −3.32. What is the PCR efficiency?

options.rationale: Incorrect. About 90% corresponds to a slope near −3.6.
Incorrect. About 110% corresponds to a slope near −3.1.
Incorrect. The slope is not a percentage; efficiency is derived as 10^(−1/slope) − 1.

questions.stem: A SYBR Green assay shows amplification in the no-template control. Which step best tells whether this signal is the true product?

options.rationale: Correct. SYBR Green binds any dsDNA; primer-dimers and non-specific products show as different melt peaks.
Incorrect. More dye does not add sequence specificity.

options.text: Report as contamination without further analysis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Primer-dimer is a common cause; a melt curve distinguishes it from the specific product.

options.text: Switch to digital PCR without a standard curve
options.rationale: Incorrect. Digital PCR changes quantification, not the dye’s non-specificity.
